alg-lower-empirical-bootstrap-quantile:
## Definition

Input a nonempty finite list $y_1,\ldots,y_B\in\mathbb R$ and $p\in[0,1]$. Sort the values with multiplicity as $y_{(1)}\le\cdots\le y_{(B)}$. If $p=0$, set $k=1$; if $p>0$, let $k$ be the least integer in $\{1,\ldots,B\}$ with $k\ge Bp$. Return
$$Q_B(p)=y_{(k)}.$$
This is the lower inverse empirical-CDF quantile, with the explicit endpoint convention $Q_B(0)=y_{(1)}$ and $Q_B(1)=y_{(B)}$. Repeated values remain repeated; no interpolation is performed. An empty list or a value of $p$ outside $[0,1]$ is inadmissible.
def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample:
## Definition

Fix integers $d,n\ge1$ and observed vectors $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$, with the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Their empirical law is the set function
$$P_n(A)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n 1\{x_i\in A\},\qquad A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d).$$

Let $\mathsf I_n=\{\omega:[n]\to[n]\}$ be the finite set of index vectors. By [[thm-cardinality-of-a-set-of-functions]], it has $n^n$ elements. Give each index vector mass $n^{-n}$; the weights sum to one, so this is a finite probability space in the sense of [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]. For $j=1,\ldots,n$, let $I_j(\omega)=\omega(j)$ and put $X_j^*(\omega)=x_{I_j(\omega)}$. The **ideal size-$n$ empirical bootstrap law conditional on the data** is the pushforward of this finite uniform law under
$\omega\longmapsto (x_{\omega(1)},\ldots,x_{\omega(n)}).$
Thus conditional probabilities are finite averages over the $n^n$ index tuples. The empirical law is a probability measure, and the bootstrap coordinates are conditionally IID with that law, by the well-definedness results listed in justified_by.

For random observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, write $\bar X_n=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i$ coordinatewise, so each coordinate is the scalar sample mean in [[def-partial-sums-and-sample-means]]. Write $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{X_i}$, using the Dirac measure [[def-dirac-measure]], and let $\bar X_n^*$ be the bootstrap mean. If $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is Borel ([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]), then
$$\hat\theta_n=g(\bar X_n),\qquad \hat\theta_n^*=g(\bar X_n^*).$$
When $X_i$ are IID ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]) with finite second moment, write $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_{1j}$ and $\Sigma_{jk}=\mathbb E[(X_{1j}-\mu_j)(X_{1k}-\mu_k)]$ ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]), and set $\theta=g(\mu)$. The functions of the data above are Borel statistics and estimators in the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; coordinatewise arithmetic preserves measurability ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]). No bootstrap validity or interval coverage is part of this definition. For $n\ge2$, the delete-one mean and plug-in statistic are
$$\bar X_{n,(-i)}=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{j\ne i}X_j,\qquad \hat\theta_{n,(-i)}=g(\bar X_{n,(-i)}).$$
lem-iid-sample-covariance-converges:
## Statement

Let $d\ge1$ be finite and let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$. Put $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_{1j}$ and $\Sigma_{jk}=\mathbb E[(X_{1j}-\mu_j)(X_{1k}-\mu_k)]$, the coordinate covariance entries from [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Define
$$\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i,\qquad \widehat\Sigma_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X_n)(X_i-\bar X_n)^T.$$
Then $\bar X_n\to\mu$ in probability and every entry of $\widehat\Sigma_n$ converges in probability to the corresponding entry of $\Sigma$.
alg-basic-bootstrap-interval:
## Definition

Input the observed estimate $\hat\theta$, a nonempty list of $B$ bootstrap estimates $\hat\theta_1^*,\ldots,\hat\theta_B^*$ generated under [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]], and $0<\alpha<1$. Let $Q_B$ be [[alg-lower-empirical-bootstrap-quantile]] and set $p=\alpha/2$. Return
$$[2\hat\theta-Q_B(1-p),\,2\hat\theta-Q_B(p)].$$
This is the reflected bootstrap-quantile interval under the declared finite-sample quantile convention. It makes no coverage claim.
alg-bias-corrected-bootstrap-interval:
## Definition

Assume AC, as required by the standard normal law. Input observed estimate $\hat\theta$, a nonempty list of $B$ bootstrap estimates $\hat\theta_1^*,\ldots,\hat\theta_B^*$ generated under [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]], and $0<\alpha<1$. Use the explicit midrank tie convention
$$\hat p_0=\frac{\#\{b:\hat\theta_b^*<\hat\theta\}+\tfrac12\#\{b:\hat\theta_b^*=\hat\theta\}}{B}.$$
Let $z_0=\Phi^{-1}(\hat p_0)$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF. Use the extended endpoint convention $\Phi^{-1}(0)=-\infty$ and $\Phi^{-1}(1)=+\infty$. With $Q_B$ from [[alg-lower-empirical-bootstrap-quantile]] and $p=\alpha/2$, return
$$\left[Q_B\!\left(\Phi(2z_0+\Phi^{-1}(p))\right),\, Q_B\!\left(\Phi(2z_0+\Phi^{-1}(1-p))\right)\right].$$
This is a finite-$B$ algorithm with an explicit tie rule; no coverage or higher-order accuracy claim is included.
alg-bootstrap-t-interval:
## Definition

Input an observed estimate $\hat\theta$, an observed standard error $\hat s>0$, and $B\ge1$ pairs $(\hat\theta_b^*,\hat s_b^*)$ with finite real $\hat\theta_b^*$ and strictly positive finite $\hat s_b^*$, produced from bootstrap samples under [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]]. If the observed or any bootstrap standard error is nonpositive or nonfinite, return **undefined**. Otherwise form
$$t_b^*=\frac{\hat\theta_b^*-\hat\theta}{\hat s_b^*},\qquad b=1,\ldots,B.$$
With $Q_B$ from [[alg-lower-empirical-bootstrap-quantile]] and $p=\alpha/2$ for a supplied $0<\alpha<1$, return
$$[\hat\theta-\hat s\,Q_B(1-p),\ \hat\theta-\hat s\,Q_B(p)].$$
The standard-error procedure is an explicit input; this algorithm alone establishes no studentized limit or coverage.
alg-percentile-bootstrap-interval:
## Definition

Input a nonempty list of $B$ bootstrap estimates $\hat\theta_1^*,\ldots,\hat\theta_B^*$ generated under the empirical bootstrap law in [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]], and $0<\alpha<1$. Let $Q_B$ be [[alg-lower-empirical-bootstrap-quantile]] and set $p=\alpha/2$. Return
$$[Q_B(p),\,Q_B(1-p)].$$
This finite-$B$ procedure uses the declared lower empirical-quantile convention. It defines endpoints only; it asserts no coverage guarantee.
lem-empirical-bootstrap-law-is-a-probabi:
## Statement

For any $n\ge1$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$, the set function
$$P_n(A)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1\{x_i\in A\},\qquad A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d),$$
is a probability measure.
thm-delete-one-jackknife-linearization-f:
## Statement

Let $X_i$ be IID $\mathbb R^d$-valued vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_{1j}$, and $\Sigma_{jk}=\mathbb E[(X_{1j}-\mu_j)(X_{1k}-\mu_k)]$ ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]). Let $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be Borel and continuously Fréchet differentiable on an open neighborhood $U$ of $\mu$; this means its Fréchet derivative exists at every point of $U$ and varies continuously there ([[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces]]). For each $x\in U$, write the row representing $Dg(x)$ in Euclidean coordinates as $\nabla g(x)^T$, and set $a=\nabla g(\mu)$; suppose $0<a^T\Sigma a<\infty$. For $n\ge2$, set $\hat\theta_n=g(\bar X_n)$, $\hat\theta_{n,(-i)}=g(\bar X_{n,(-i)})$, $\bar\theta_{n,(-)}=n^{-1}\sum_i\hat\theta_{n,(-i)}$, and
$$V_{J,n}=\frac{n-1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(\hat\theta_{n,(-i)}-\bar\theta_{n,(-)})^2,\qquad p_{n,i}=n\hat\theta_n-(n-1)\hat\theta_{n,(-i)}.$$
Then
$$\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\left|p_{n,i}-\{\hat\theta_n+a^T(X_i-\bar X_n)\}\right|^2\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability},\qquad nV_{J,n}\longrightarrow a^T\Sigma a\quad\text{in probability}.$$
The neighborhood $C^1$ condition is used for the deletion secants; differentiability at $\mu$ alone is not asserted to give this jackknife conclusion.
lem-finite-bootstrap-cdf-supremum-is-mea:
## Statement

Let $n,d\ge1$, let $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ be a measurable $(\mathbb R^d)^n$-valued random vector, and fix $a\in\mathbb R^d$. For each finite index tuple $\omega=(i_1,\ldots,i_n)\in\mathsf I_n=\{1,\ldots,n\}^n$, define the projected centered bootstrap-mean value
$$R_{n,\omega}=\sqrt n\,a^T\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{\ell=1}^n X_{i_\ell}-\bar X_n\right),\qquad \bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.$$
The finite-index conditional bootstrap CDF is
$$F_n^*(t)=n^{-n}\sum_{\omega\in\mathsf I_n}1\{R_{n,\omega}\le t\}.$$
For every fixed continuous cumulative distribution function $G:\mathbb R\to[0,1]$, the supremum
$$D_n=\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|F_n^*(t)-G(t)|$$
is a measurable real random variable.
alg-delete-one-jackknife-acceleration:
## Definition

Input $n\ge2$ real delete-one estimates $\hat\theta_{(-1)},\ldots,\hat\theta_{(-n)}$. Compute
$$\bar\theta_{(-)}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\hat\theta_{(-i)},\qquad d_i=\bar\theta_{(-)}-\hat\theta_{(-i)},\qquad S_2=\sum_i d_i^2.$$
If $S_2=0$, return **undefined**. Otherwise return the jackknife acceleration
$$\hat a_J=\frac{\sum_i d_i^3}{6S_2^{3/2}}.$$
The output is the finite-sample acceleration input used by the BCa procedure. For a $C^1$ function of an IID mean, [[thm-delete-one-jackknife-linearization-for-smooth-statistics]] proves the first-order jackknife variance relation; this algorithm and that first-order theorem make no BCa coverage claim.
lem-finite-index-bootstrap-sample-is-con:
## Statement

For fixed data $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$, the coordinates of the finite-index bootstrap sample in [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]] are independent and each has law $P_n$.
alg-bca-bootstrap-interval:
## Definition

Assume AC. Input observed estimate $\hat\theta$, a nonempty list of $B$ bootstrap estimates, $n\ge2$ delete-one estimates, and $0<\alpha<1$. The bootstrap estimates are generated under [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]]. Compute
$$\hat p_0=\frac{\#\{b:\hat\theta_b^*<\hat\theta\}+\tfrac12\#\{b:\hat\theta_b^*=\hat\theta\}}{B},\qquad \hat z_0=\Phi^{-1}(\hat p_0),$$
using the midrank tie rule and extended endpoint convention $\Phi^{-1}(0)=-\infty$, $\Phi^{-1}(1)=+\infty$, and compute $\hat a_J$ by [[alg-delete-one-jackknife-acceleration]].

If $\hat p_0\in\{0,1\}$ or $\hat a_J$ is undefined, return **undefined**. Otherwise, for $\gamma\in\{\alpha/2,1-\alpha/2\}$ set
$$z_\gamma=\Phi^{-1}(\gamma),\qquad p_\gamma=\Phi\!\left(z_0+\frac{z_0+z_\gamma}{1-\hat a_J(z_0+z_\gamma)}\right),$$
where $z_0=\Phi^{-1}(\hat p_0)$. If either denominator is zero or $p_{\alpha/2}\ge p_{1-\alpha/2}$, return **undefined**. Otherwise return $[Q_B(p_{\alpha/2}),Q_B(p_{1-\alpha/2})]$, using [[alg-lower-empirical-bootstrap-quantile]]. These instructions define a finite-sample procedure only; no BCa coverage theorem is asserted.
thm-conditional-iid-bootstrap-clt-for-em:
## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be IID $\mathbb R^d$-valued vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean $\mu$, and covariance $\Sigma$. Fix $a\in\mathbb R^d$ such that $\sigma^2=a^T\Sigma a>0$. For the finite-index empirical bootstrap in [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]], let $\bar X_n^*$ be the bootstrap mean and define the conditional CDF
$$F_n^*(x)=\mathbb P^*\!\left(\sqrt n\,a^T(\bar X_n^*-\bar X_n)\le x\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n\right).$$
Then
$$D_n:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}\left|F_n^*(x)-\Phi_\sigma(x)\right|\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability},$$
where $\Phi_\sigma$ is the CDF of $N(0,\sigma^2)$. The assumption $\sigma^2>0$ is needed for the normalized Lindeberg–Feller step.
thm-iid-bootstrap-validity-for-smooth-st:
## Statement

Assume AC. Let $X_i$ be IID $\mathbb R^d$-valued vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean $\mu$, and covariance $\Sigma$. Let $g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be Borel and Fréchet differentiable at $\mu$, with derivative $a^T$, and assume
$$0<\sigma^2:=a^T\Sigma a<\infty.$$
Set $\theta=g(\mu)$, $\hat\theta_n=g(\bar X_n)$, and $\hat\theta_n^*=g(\bar X_n^*)$ for the finite-index empirical bootstrap in [[def-iid-empirical-bootstrap-sample]]. Then
$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2),$$
and, for every fixed $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb P^*\!\left(\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n^*-\hat\theta_n)\le x\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n\right)\longrightarrow\Phi_\sigma(x)\quad\text{in probability},$$
where $\Phi_\sigma$ is the CDF of $N(0,\sigma^2)$. Thus the ideal conditional bootstrap law and the sampling law have the same first-order limit with the stated centering and $\sqrt n$ scaling. This theorem does not imply coverage of any interval algorithm.
